top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: Data were extracted using a standardised form adapted from the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (version 6.3) [27], with pre-specified units/ scales (e.g., VAS 0-10 or 0-100, ODI 0-100, MSK-HQ 0-56, EQ-5D index) recorded as reported. Extracted items included authors, year, country, design, sample, intervention/comparator, outcomes, measurement tools, sources of funding, declared conflicts of interest, and key quantitative results. Participants were counted once per unique study or cohort to avoid double counting when the same cohort was reported across linked publications (e.g., primary study and linked economic evaluation) or contributed data to multiple outcomes. For transparency, all study-level quantitative results used to populate the SoF are reproduced verbatim in Additional Tables S1-S7, with units and time windows preserved. Two reviewers (MaF and EB) independently extracted data and reconciled discrepancies by consensus.

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: A total of 90,401 adults with musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) were analyzed (15,017 in direct access [DA] models; 75,384 in GP-referred pathways). This figure represents unique participants per cohort; the higher total of 91,599 sometimes derivable from supplementary tables results from summing sample sizes across linked publications and outcome-specific reports from the same underlying cohorts (see Methods). Most studies originated from the UK, Sweden, and North America, with one French pilot. MSDs mainly included low back and neck pain, osteoarthritis, and tendinopathies. DA models ranged from fully autonomous first-contact physiotherapy to structured triage-based services. Funding for 12 of the 17 included reports was provided by public or non-profit institutional grants (e.g., NIHR, Versus Arthritis, regional health services, or university grants). One study was funded by a combination of industry and professional association grants, and four reports did not state a funding source. Regarding competing interests, 12 reports explicitly declared no conflicts of interest. Two reports declared minor editorial conflicts unlikely to influence the outcomes, and three reports did not include a competing interest statement.

top_evidence.section: Methods > Study Design And Reporting Framework
top_evidence.text: This systematic review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 [24]. In accordance with PRISMA, we prepared outcome-specific Summary of Findings tables (SoF) that collate study-level results per outcome and are provided as Additional Tables S1-S7. The protocol was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; ID 897ub; 15 August 2024, available at h t t p s : / / o s f . i o/ 8 9 7 u b / ) [25]. The completed PRISMA 2020 checklist is available in Additional file 1.

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: Population: adults (≥ 18 years) with non-specific MSDs (i.e., musculoskeletal conditions without identified specific pathology such as fracture, inflammatory arthritis, or malignancy) managed in primary care; Intervention: DA to physiotherapy. Comparator: GP-referred pathway (referral-based usual care); Primary outcome: GP workload (number/frequency of GP consultations); Secondary outcomes: medication/imaging prescriptions, patientreported outcomes (pain, function, QoL), direct/indirect costs, safety; Designs included: RCTs and observational comparative studies (cohort, case-control, quasi-experimental). This combination was chosen to capture both efficacy data from experimental designs (RCTs) and realworld organizational impacts (observational studies) often unavailable in experimental settings. Systematic reviews were excluded from the synthesis and used for context only. Qualitative-only reports, case series, protocols, and non-peer-reviewed documents were excluded. A consolidated PICO framework mapping populations, interventions/comparators, and outcomes across included studies is presented in Additional file 3.

top_evidence.document_title: Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care: consequences for general practitioner workload, resource use, and organisation of care
top_evidence.text: Given clinical and methodological heterogeneity across designs, settings, and outcomes, we conducted a narrative synthesis. Where available, we report effect measures with 95% CIs and p-values. We did not perform formal small-study or publication-bias tests because no meta-analysis was undertaken; instead, we qualitatively appraised potential reporting/publication biases and reflected these concerns within GRADE. Results from secondary research (systematic reviews) were used for context only and were not recombined with primary studies to avoid double counting.
